The documents are public records and openly licensed or public-domain material from the United States (federal agencies and the Senate, state agencies and a state judiciary, the District of Columbia, counties, cities, a town, a public utility district and a state university, and companies' papers in public files), the United Kingdom, Ireland, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, India and bodies of the European Union, with eleven historical papers of 1875 to 1988, four of them New Zealand papers from an archive's, a library's, a gallery's and a museum's collections and two wartime notices from the National Archives Catalog, fetched from their sources at evaluation time and never committed; each entry names its source and licence. Twenty-eight have a stated basis for reuse: eleven US government works and two US government forms filled in by a private party (real8-form-04, real8-contract-01); two under the Open Government Licence, two under the CC BY 4.0 licence of New Zealand Crown copyright and one under CC BY 2.0; four that their holders mark as having no known copyright restrictions (the New Jersey State Library, the Hocken Collections, the Sarjeant Gallery and MOTAT); three filings on the Companies House register, which imposes no rules on how register information is used (the forms are Crown copyright; nothing is stated for the companies' own words); and three under their publishers' own terms (the Government of Canada's non-commercial reproduction terms, and the European Banking Authority's and a Government of India site's permission to reproduce with the source acknowledged). The other twenty-seven are public records with no licence stated, which is not sparing and is said plainly: notices, minutes, memoranda, filings and invoices are almost never released under a licence. Twenty of them are a public body's own paper, published by that body or released by it or by another public body (seven notices, three sets of minutes, two memoranda, three letters, two parish councils' returns, an order form, a memorandum of understanding and a certificate with its filing); six are a private party's paper in a public body's file or freedom-of-information release (a company's letter in a regulator's docket, a residents' federation's letter in a city clerk's file, an employer's layoff notice filed with a state, and three suppliers' invoices); and one is an archival file whose first page, a senator's letter, is a US government work and whose other two are a copy of a banker's letter of 1935 (real8-letter-12). Six of the twenty-seven come from sites that assert copyright and give no reuse terms (a county's and a township's notices, a court's notice, an election notice that a town council republished, a utility district's and a university senate's minutes); none is under terms that ask that permission be sought before reproduction, the ground on which two documents were left out. It holds 55 documents: 18 letters, 12 notices, 6 invoices, 1 purchase order, 2 statements, 5 forms, 3 contracts (a lease and two memoranda of understanding), 1 report, 4 memoranda and 3 sets of minutes, in 46 PDFs (27 with a native text layer, one of them rebuilt from a scan and one with its signature blocks pasted in as pictures; 19 scanned or image-only, 11 of them with an OCR layer and 8 without one, one of those ending in a born-digital page), 6 JPEG images, 2 DOCX files and 1 XLSX workbook. Eleven are historical and 44 modern; one prints no date of its own and is for review; the gold readiness is ready for 22, either for 32 and needs_review for 1. It was gathered after every rule written so far, and no rule or threshold has been written from it. Each gold answer was written from the document alone, before Intern read any of them, and was independently second-read: three second readers, one for each gatherer's group, named every document before opening its gold and listed where they disagreed, raising 117 points of disagreement on the 64 documents first gathered (60 and four spares; 88 of the points concern the 55 kept and 7 a group as a whole). Each was adjudicated from the document's own text and the conventions of the earlier samples: 53 settled as the reader asked, 35 left as the gatherer had them, 16 by widening the acceptable answers, 10 by removing accepted answers (in nine letters the further 'between' spellings of one side, beside which no 'between' answer could meet the scorer's party-role check, and on a spreadsheet a bare type that also matched a bank statement), and 3 moot because their document was dropped; the adjudicators added 15 corrections and notes that no reader had raised. Four of the 64 were dropped at adjudication, three on licence grounds (a charity's notice and another charity's minutes on their own sites, and a publisher's subscription agreement with its general terms, released with the originator's rights reserved) and one as a duplicate (a second memorandum of one city to its council from one archive), and one spare was not used (a company's submission from the host and to the recipient of real8-letter-15); three spares and one document gathered at adjudication took their places, and that one (real8-contract-03) had no blind second reading: the assembler read it against its gold and agreed in every scored field. Of the 60 that remained the assembler left out five to reach 55: a regulator's letter and a state department's memorandum whose sites allow reproduction only after permission is asked, draft minutes at an address their council replaces once the minutes are approved, a company's certificate that was the fourth paper from one reading room and whose handwritten year is an overwritten blot, and a second billhead from one library, whose host had answered fetch.py with HTTP 429. The assembler also rewrote the party-role rows of four entries (real8-invoice-01, real8-purchase_order-01, real8-contract-01, real8-contract-02) under the names their pages print whole, so that their accepted 'between' answers meet the scorer's party-role check, which as adjudicated none of the first two's and not all of the others' could; no accepted name, type or date changed, and three accepted 'between' spellings still miss that check (the committee's English name, which real8-invoice-01 does not print, in two sets, and 'U.S. Government' on real8-contract-01). The assembler left the date role of the undated real8-notice-11 empty, as sample-heldout5 does, and added to the notes of real8-letter-02 and real8-notice-09 printed words, and to those of real8-memo-03 the expansion of an abbreviation, that their gold already used. Four hosts refused or rate-limited some scripted requests while the set was being read (www.usitc.gov and townofastatula.com by client string, cbcindia.gov.in and hocken.recollect.co.nz after repeated requests); every document was fetched by fetch.py and matched its pins on 15 November 2026.

documents.title: United States Trade Representative's letter of November 30, 2018 to Mexico's Secretary of Economy confirming an agreement on Section 232 measures for passenger vehicles, light trucks and auto parts, a USMCA side letter (born-digital PDF, 2 pages)
documents.notes: Two pages of plain typed text with no letterhead, logo or signature. Dated 'November 30, 2018' in the centre; to 'The Honorable Ildefonso Guajardo Villarreal, Secretary of Economy, Mexico City, United Mexican States', 'Dear Secretary Guajardo:'. 'I have the honor to confirm the following agreement reached between the Government of the United States ("the United States") and the Government of the United Mexican States ("Mexico")': if the United States imposes a measure under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 on passenger vehicles, light trucks or auto parts, it will exclude 2,600,000 passenger vehicles a year, light trucks, and auto parts worth 108 billion U.S. dollars a year from Mexico; goods that do not qualify as originating pay no more than 'the United States' MFN applied rate in effect on August 1, 2018'. It names the USMCA ('the Agreement Between the United States of America, the United Mexican States, and Canada') and 'NAFTA 1994'. 'I have the honor to propose that this letter and your letter of confirmation in reply shall constitute an agreement between the United States and Mexico, which shall enter into force on the date of your letter in reply.' Closing 'Sincerely,' and, typed, 'Ambassador Robert E. Lighthizer, United States Trade Representative': the only place the sender is named. USTR's site lists it among the USMCA side letters ('MX-US Side Letter on 232'), a title the letter does not print. PDF metadata: created and last modified at 21:06 on 29 November 2018, US Eastern time (D:20181129210611-05'00'), the evening before the letter's date; in UTC that instant is 30 November. Because the letter records an agreement between two governments and proposes that the exchange constitute it, the two governments are accepted with 'between' as well as the sender with 'from' and the addressee with 'to'. Traps: the rate reference date of August 1, 2018; the metadata date a day early; the years 1962 and 1994; the two officials as persons; Canada, a party to the USMCA but not to this letter; the absence of any letterhead.

documents.notes: A photograph of one ruled sheet. Printed head in outline capitals 'MAIN NORTH ROAD, WAIKOUAITI,'; a dotted line begun with a printed 'M' on which is written 'Waikouaiti Library Committee', and at the right the date in ink on a partly printed line, 'Nov 26th 1875' (the '187' is printed). Then 'Dr. to WILLIAM MILL, TIMBER MERCHANT.' with 'DOORS, SASHES, ARCHITRAVES, IRONMONGERY, OILS, PAINTS, &c., &c.' at the left. The entries are in a clerk's hand: 'March 1st To Amount Rendered £265 15 6', 'Interest from Mar 1st to July 1st 1875 @ 10 pc 8 1 8' (273 17 2), 'July 1/75 By Cash on Account 65 15 6' (208 1 8), 'Interest from July 1 to Decr 1st 75 - 5 mo @ 10 pc 8 13 -', total 216 14 8. Across the entries someone has written diagonally that the account was passed for payment, with a signature and 'Chair'; at the foot 'Settled in full' with the signature 'W. Mill', beside a purple New Zealand one-penny stamp duty stamp cancelled in ink, and a pencilled sum at the bottom right. It is an account rendered that became a receipt once settled; gold names it as the bill it was issued as and accepts the other readings. Its only date is the day the bill was made out (it charges interest to 1 December 1875, so it was settled later): the date is the bill's, and its role an invoice date. The customer is accepted beside the issuer in a 'between' name, as the newest earlier samples accept an invoice's customer, and is a trap alone. Traps: the customer written first; the dates inside the entries (1 March, 1 July and 1 December 1875), the last of them after the date of the bill; the endorsement and the signatures; the place name read as the issuer.
